title: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
desc: Requires contextual quality, reproducibility, contamination control, agent diagnosis, cost accounting and independent safety testing.

kps.k: Benchmark scores support bounded comparisons, not automatic claims of professional competence or deployment safety.
kps.d: The cluster challenges the inference from success on a test dataset to dependable performance in practice, rather than rejecting benchmarking. The Law of Evaluation recognises standardisation, scalability and reproducibility; AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark argues that particular datasets cannot establish context-independent capabilities. Both question treating bar-exam performance as evidence of legal skill. NIST’s draft offers a practical formulation: define the intended measurement and decision first, then substantiate why the selected tasks support that inference.

qs.q: Benchmarks have gained popularity as they provide standardized, scalable, and reproducible metrics across models, teams, and time.10
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Legal AI evaluation must assess contextual quality and human–AI workflows, not isolated accuracy alone.
kps.d: Guha and colleagues argue that contracts, summaries and advice often lack universally accepted quality metrics and require costly, context-sensitive expert assessment. An eviction chatbot needs appropriate tone and clarity as well as correctness. They also distinguish accurate outputs from practical value: excessive checking can erase benefits, while confidentiality limits access to actual workflows. NIST similarly directs human-interactive and subjective questions toward methods beyond automated benchmarks, including field testing. These arguments identify evidence gaps; they do not establish productivity gains or losses.

qs.a: There is No Free Benchmark: An Institutional View of Legal AI Benchmarking · Academia · 2026

qs.q: Human in the loop: tasks require repeated interaction or open-ended use, and/or the evaluation objective intends to measure the AI system in conjunction with human operator(s) or other affected parties.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Reproducibility, statistical validity and construct validity require separate checks.
kps.d: BetterBench applies 46 quality criteria to 24 benchmarks and reports that 14 lacked repeated evaluations or uncertainty reporting; 17 lacked easy-to-run replication scripts, while four supplied only partial scripts. Its quality scores do not establish application fitness or construct validity. Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox warns that even reported error bars can be invalid and demonstrates mixed-model analysis of 22 LLMs on three benchmarks, without quantifying the estimation benefit in the supplied material. Evaluating General-Purpose AI with Psychometrics separately examines consistency across items, raters and datasets and whether tests measure their intended constructs.

qs.q: Yet, 14 out of 24 benchmarks did not perform multiple evaluations of the same model or report statistical significance or uncertainty of results.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: For example, one approach to reporting benchmark performance is to calculate a simple average score with standard error across all test items and trials2 — but this approach can produce statistically invalid error bars.
qs.a: Expanding the AI Evaluation Toolbox with Statistical Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

kps.k: Contamination, overfitting and saturation weaken scores, but safeguards involve trade-offs.
kps.d: The sources distinguish training on test data, optimising agents around known test samples and benchmarks becoming too easy to differentiate systems. AI Agents That Matter reports missing held-out tests in many agent benchmarks and recommends considering secret test sets; its perfect lookup-table result is hypothetical. NIST recommends hidden or newly generated data. Guha and colleagues stress that disclosure enables scrutiny but increases contamination and replacement costs, while BetterBench notes that dynamic tests can reduce comparability. Narrow specialisation is not inherently defective: its adequacy depends on the agent’s intended scope.

qs.q: Yet, surprisingly, we find that many agent benchmarks do not include held-out test sets.
qs.a: AI Agents That Matter · Academia · 2024

qs.q: 8) issues but reduce result comparability and are easier to implement for some tasks (e.g., adding numbers) than others.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Agent evaluation needs execution-level diagnosis, cost accounting and independent safety tests.
kps.d: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents argues that offline next-action tests miss cascading errors because actions do not change subsequent observations. It recommends dynamic environments, step-level assessment and controlled comparisons that separate the underlying model from the software coordinating its tools, memory and planning. Task success and repeatability do not establish privacy or access-control compliance, and capability scores can conceal prohibitive operating costs. Agent-as-a-Judge likewise proposes process-aware evaluation of development work; the supplied excerpt does not demonstrate labour savings or the effectiveness of automated judges.

qs.q: While scalable, these fail to capture the cascading effects of errors: incorrect actions have no downstream consequences, missing compounding failures that can ultimately cause task failure.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: A benchmark that can evaluate the entire development process—ideally in a way that can help understand the degree to which current AI methods can reduce human labour—is missing.
qs.a: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Benchmark credibility depends on incentives and institutional access as well as technical design.
kps.d: The interdisciplinary review and Guha and colleagues argue that sales, publication and leaderboard incentives can favour selective tasks, configurations and reporting. Guha and colleagues illustrate the problem with Paxton AI’s advertised accuracy above 94% on a narrow explicit-overruling task that simple bag-of-words models reportedly handled nearly perfectly; this does not establish broad legal reliability. Aggregate scores can also conceal subgroup failures. These accounts identify risks and reported examples, not universal vendor misconduct. Benchmark coverage itself affects competition: excluding smaller products can deny them opportunities to demonstrate quality and leave their users uninformed.

qs.q: We identify a strong incentive gap in the use of benchmarks between academic researchers (who may for example primarily be interested in methods development), corporations (who are driven by economic incentives in their use and development of benchmarks), and regulators (who have a particular responsibility to consider practical utility and potential downstream effects).
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: benchmarking matters, compare the information produced A second illustration comes from Paxton AI issuing a press by benchmarking to other kinds of information about AI, and release with the headline “Paxton AI achieves 94%+ accuracy formalize the notion of “legibility.” on Stanford Hallucination Benchmark.” The task was a tool to classify whether cases are positively or negatively associated 1.1.

kps.k: The main tension concerns how far benchmark reform can go, not whether evaluation matters.
kps.d: The sources largely converge, but differ in emphasis. BetterBench, NIST and the statistical and psychometric contributions develop ways to improve measurement. AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark rejects simply enlarging general benchmarks as a remedy for unsupported claims of generality. The Law of Evaluation welcomes broader safety and impact metrics while retaining its contextual objections. Can We Trust AI Benchmarks concludes that quantitative tests cannot currently supply policymakers’ primary assurances, but does not reject eventual AI safety assurance. Its non-exhaustive, criticism-focused literature review does not establish the effectiveness or adoption of proposed mitigations.

qs.q: This is not a question of “fixing”, “improving” or “expanding” the current “general” benchmarks — after all, the solution to addressing the issues inherent to the “Everything in the Whole Wide World” museum is not to add more rooms.
qs.a: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark · Academia · 2021

qs.q: Benchmarks now exist that take a more holistic view of a system’s performance, but even such welcome improvements still suffer from the other limitations discussed.
qs.a: The Law of Evaluation: Beyond Benchmarks for AI Governance · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Practical proposals combine purpose-specific evidence, benchmark quality standards and independent oversight.
kps.d: For procurement and deployment, the proposed approach pairs documented, reproducible tests with relevant human or non-AI baselines, realistic workflows, failure analysis and complementary red-teaming or field testing. For governance, the interdisciplinary review favours standardising how benchmark trustworthiness is assessed rather than imposing uniform metrics. Guha and colleagues propose independent programmes, consortia or targeted grants according to resources, while BetterBench suggests possible reporting and procurement requirements. These remain proposed arrangements, not evaluated policy outcomes; strict requirements may burden less-resourced researchers, and no single institutional model resolves all trade-offs.

qs.q: Having relevant baseline or reference measures is beneficial when an evaluation seeks to compare the performance of an AI system to the performance of alternative approaches (e.g., humans only, prior non-AI automation, humans assisted by AI, or random chance).
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: But we do need standardised methods for assessing the trustworthiness of benchmarks from an applied and regulatory perspective.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The sole legal-tech vendor record, JudgmentBench, contains only bibliographic references and no substantive claims, methods, findings, qualifications or recommendations. It therefore provides no basis for determining whether this source accepts, extends, redirects or rejects the proposition that valid evaluation requires contextual quality, reproducibility, contamination control, agent-level diagnosis, cost accounting and independent safety testing. This is an evidentiary limitation specific to the supplied excerpt and should not be generalized to legal-tech vendors as a group.

The selected academia and research sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that benchmark scores are bounded evidence and cannot, by themselves, establish professional competence, real-world performance or deployment safety. They materially develop that proposition by specifying complementary safeguards: lifecycle quality standards, separate tests of reproducibility, reliability and construct validity, contamination and overfitting controls, contextual and human–AI workflow assessment, execution-level agent diagnosis, cost and compliance metrics, controlled attribution between models and agent harnesses, and independent or consortium-based oversight. Common reasons include mismatch between static tests and deployment conditions, prompt sensitivity, leakage and saturation, coarse aggregate or final-outcome metrics, and incentives that can favour selective tasks or reporting. Material variation concerns the appropriate remedy. Some sources seek to improve benchmarks through checklists, psychometrics, dynamic environments and held-out tests; another argues that unsupported claims of generality require tightly scoped benchmarks plus alternative evaluation methods rather than simply larger general benchmarks. Agent-focused work prioritises trajectories, cascading failures, operational costs and safety, while legal-AI work stresses expert judgment, human use and institutional design. The safeguards also conflict: secrecy can reduce contamination but limit scrutiny; dynamic tests can improve realism but reduce comparability; and demanding standards can burden less-resourced researchers. Several contributions are methodological or governance proposals rather than demonstrated improvements in deployment outcomes. This characterisation applies only to the curated sources supplied, not academia or researchers generally.

qs.q: However, there is a potential risk of misinterpretation of our results; our assessment only provides minimum quality assurances and is not sufficient to assess the suitability of a benchmark for a concrete use case.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Future work should develop controlled evaluation protocols that vary each factor independently, enabling systematic comparison and isolating the contribution of individual components, whether LLM capabilities, harness design, or specific modules such as memory or planning, to overall agent performance.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The supplied regulators, courts and professional-bodies sources accept the proposition that benchmark scores provide bounded evidence rather than automatic proof of professional competence, real-world performance or deployment safety. They materially develop that proposition by specifying safeguards at several levels: NIST supplies purpose-specific practices for defining constructs and intended uses, establishing valid task-to-claim inferences, using realistic baselines, controlling contamination, supporting reproducibility, accounting for operational costs and supplementing automation with human or field evaluation; the statistical-methods paper isolates statistical validity and proposes mixed-model analysis to improve uncertainty and performance estimation; and the interdisciplinary review adds construct, cultural, incentive, regulatory and institutional dimensions, including standards for assessing benchmark trustworthiness and complementary red-teaming or bug-bounty methods. Material internal variation lies mainly in scope and confidence. NIST is practical and method-focused but expressly limited to using existing automated benchmarks. The statistical paper offers a narrower technical remedy and does not address workflow, safety-testing or governance safeguards. The interdisciplinary review is broader and more sceptical about present regulatory reliance, judging quantitative benchmarks currently unsuitable as primary assurances while maintaining that stronger assurance systems may eventually be developed and noting that proposed mitigations remain unproven. These curated sources therefore converge on reforming and supplementing evaluation, not rejecting it, but should not be read as representing all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: The design, execution, and reporting of an evaluation all depend on the evaluation objectives, including what should be measured (the measurement construct) and intended uses for the results produced.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition that benchmark safeguards are necessary because benchmark scores warrant only bounded, context-specific inferences rather than general claims about capability or deployment safety. Its central reasoning is construct validity: performance on a particular dataset, metric and evaluation practice cannot establish context-independent competence. It also supports retaining benchmarks for concrete, well-scoped tasks while supplementing broader capability assessment with audits, adversarial testing, output analysis and related methods. The source further reinforces the cluster’s institutional concerns by arguing that research and marketing incentives can exaggerate benchmark significance, and that aggregate scores can hide subgroup failures. The main internal qualification is therefore not opposition to benchmarking but a distinction between legitimate, contextualised use and decontextualised claims of generality. Compared with the full synthesis, its coverage is narrower: it anticipates contextual quality, alternative testing and incentive problems, but does not substantially develop later safeguards concerning reproducibility, contamination control, agent execution diagnosis or cost accounting. Because the period contains one curated source, this assessment characterises that source rather than the prevalence of the view in the wider literature.

qs.q: Benchmarking, appropriately deployed, is not about winning a contest but more about surveying a landscape — the more we can re-frame, contextualize and appropriately scope these datasets, the more useful they will become as an informative dimension to more impactful algorithmic development and alternative evaluation methods (see Appendix A).
qs.a: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark · Academia · 2021

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources consistently accept the proposition that benchmark results are bounded, context-dependent evidence rather than automatic proof of real-world capability or deployment safety. They materially develop that proposition in complementary ways: BetterBench supplies a lifecycle-based quality framework covering reproducibility, uncertainty, documentation, contamination and maintenance; the psychometrics source separates reliability from validity and broadens error analysis across items, raters and datasets; Agent-as-a-Judge proposes process-aware evaluation of intermediate stages in long-horizon agent work; and AI Agents That Matter identifies agent-specific overfitting and recommends held-out, potentially secret test sets. Material variation concerns the remedy and evidential maturity rather than the core diagnosis. BetterBench focuses on minimum quality assurance and possible governance uses while disclaiming construct validity and use-case fitness; psychometrics concentrates on measurement theory; Agent-as-a-Judge offers design proposals rather than demonstrated labour-saving results; and AI Agents That Matter stresses safeguards while treating specialisation as acceptable when aligned with an agent’s intended scope. Together, these sources strengthen the cluster’s case for contextual, reproducible and agent-aware evaluation, while preserving the trade-offs between secrecy and scrutiny, comparability and dynamic testing, and assurance requirements and access to benchmark-development resources.

qs.q: However, there is a potential risk of misinterpretation of our results; our assessment only provides minimum quality assurances and is not sufficient to assess the suitability of a benchmark for a concrete use case.
qs.a: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Second, it should emphasize the development process, not just final outcomes (e.g., pass@1 rates offer limited feedback and fail to highlight intermediate problems).
qs.a: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The selected 2025 sources accept the proposition that benchmark scores provide only bounded evidence and materially extend its safeguards for adoption at scale. Both argue that static, aggregate task-success measures can miss real-world failure modes and cannot by themselves establish capability or safety. Their common reasons include weak construct validity, outdated or contaminated tests, limited reproducibility, inadequate diagnosis of errors, and omission of contextual safety concerns. They also treat reform as involving trade-offs rather than as a completed solution: human validation can improve validity but constrain scalability, while proposed dynamic and complementary methods remain incompletely validated. Material variation lies in emphasis. The agent-evaluation survey develops an operational framework centred on dynamic environments, execution trajectories, cost, policy compliance, and separating model from harness contributions. The interdisciplinary review instead broadens the analysis to incentives, culture, regulation, data provenance and benchmark-level trustworthiness standards. Both primarily offer recommendations and syntheses, not demonstrated evidence that these safeguards have achieved reliable adoption at scale.

qs.q: While scalable, these fail to capture the cascading effects of errors: incorrect actions have no downstream consequences, missing compounding failures that can ultimately cause task failure.
qs.a: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents · Academia · 2025

qs.q: In line with previous studies [Jones et al., 2024], our meta-review suggests that the field of quantitative benchmarking is currently ill-suited to single-handedly (or primarily) provide the safety and capability assurances requested by policy makers.
qs.a: Can We Trust AI Benchmarks? An Interdisciplinary Review of Current Issues in AI Evaluation · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 sources collectively accept the proposition’s core: benchmark scores are useful for bounded comparison but cannot alone establish real-world performance, professional competence or deployment safety. They materially develop that proposition in complementary ways. NIST translates it into purpose-specific practice—define the construct and intended use, justify task-to-claim inferences, use relevant baselines, control contamination, account for operational costs, and supplement automation with human red-teaming or field testing. The statistical-methods paper narrows in on uncertainty, warning that conventional error bars may be invalid and proposing generalized linear mixed models to improve estimation. The legal-AI institutional analysis extends beyond test design to incentives, access and governance, offering resource-dependent models for independent programmes, consortia and grants while emphasising trade-offs among transparency, contamination, cost and competitive inclusion. The Law of Evaluation more directly supports rather than extends the proposition, stressing contextual mismatch, leakage, saturation and narrow metrics. Material variation therefore concerns the remedy and level of analysis—methodological guidance, statistical correction, or institutional design—not whether evaluation matters. JudgmentBench cannot be placed because the supplied excerpt is bibliography-only. Because this is a curated set, these positions should not be treated as representative of all 2026 sources or stakeholder groups.

qs.q: Comprehensive: conducting evaluations via multiple methods and modalities (e.g., automated benchmarking, human red-teaming, field testing, etc.) may be more expensive but can improve assurance.
qs.a: NIST AI 800-2 ipd: Practices for Automated Benchmark Evaluations of Language Models · Regulators & courts · 2026
